issues.legal_issue: A higher court may not reverse an acquittal and convict where the prosecution evidence, considered as a whole, leaves reasonable doubt about guilt.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after finding the eyewitness accounts inconsistent and the prosecution case doubtful.
The High Court set aside the acquittal and convicted some accused under Sections 302 read with 34, 324 read with 149, and 323 of the IPC.

The Supreme Court found serious contradictions in the eyewitness evidence, uncertainty about when and where the complaint was recorded, inconsistent accounts of the incident and seizure of weapons, and investigative lapses.
The Supreme Court concluded that the witnesses were not trustworthy and that the evidence did not prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in reversing the acquittal; the Supreme Court set aside its judgment and restored the trial court’s acquittal.
issues.legal_principle: An accused is presumed innocent unless guilt is proved beyond reasonable doubt. An appellate court cannot sustain a conviction when the prosecution evidence, viewed as a whole, is not trustworthy and leaves reasonable doubt. The offences at issue were charged under Sections 302 read with 34, 324 read with 149, and 323 of the IPC. The Supreme Court did not rely on an earlier case in stating this principle; the cases cited by counsel were not adopted as the basis of its reasoning.

rule.if: acquittal_appeal and material_witness_contradictions and unreliable_prosecution_evidence and (investigative_lapses or evidentiary_uncertainty)

predicates.acquittal_appeal: A criminal appeal challenged a higher court’s decision to set aside an acquittal and convict the accused.
predicates.material_witness_contradictions: Prosecution witnesses gave conflicting accounts on material aspects of the incident, the complaint, or the investigation.
predicates.unreliable_prosecution_evidence: The court found that the prosecution witnesses’ evidence was not trustworthy.
predicates.investigative_lapses: The investigation included significant omissions or inconsistencies affecting the prosecution case.
predicates.evidentiary_uncertainty: The evidence left unresolved doubt about the prosecution’s account or the identity and use of the alleged weapons.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges the reversal of an acquittal and material contradictions make the prosecution evidence unreliable, investigative lapses or other evidentiary uncertainty support restoring the acquittal.

issues.legal_issue: Material contradictions and clear improvements in prosecution testimony make it unsafe to rely on that testimony when they create serious doubt about its truthfulness.
material_facts: The eyewitnesses differed about the time of the incident, who was present, when police arrived, where the complaint was recorded, and how the weapons were seized.
A witness gave differing accounts of who assaulted him, and some accused were named only in later statements.
The eyewitness accounts also differed on injuries and events at the scene, and one account of injuries inflicted on the deceased was inconsistent with the medical evidence.
issues.conclusion: The serious contradictions went to the root of the prosecution case, so the eyewitness evidence was not a safe basis for conviction and the accused were entitled to the benefit of doubt.
issues.legal_principle: Ordinary discrepancies may occur between an incident and testimony given later, but contradictions that create serious doubt about witness truthfulness, show clear improvement, and go to the root of the case make reliance unsafe. The accused remain entitled to the benefit of doubt where the prosecution fails to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The Supreme Court did not rely on an earlier case for this principle.

rule.if: criminal_prosecution and material_testimony_contradictions and (clear_testimony_improvements or contradictions_create_serious_doubt)

predicates.criminal_prosecution: A person was prosecuted for a criminal offence.
predicates.material_testimony_contradictions: Prosecution witnesses gave conflicting accounts on matters material to the incident or the accused’s alleged conduct.
predicates.clear_testimony_improvements: A witness added or changed material details in a later account compared with an earlier account.
predicates.contradictions_create_serious_doubt: The conflicts in the testimony caused serious doubt about whether the witnesses were truthful.

issues.definition: In a criminal prosecution, material contradictions make testimony unsafe as a basis for conviction when they show clear improvements or create serious doubt.

issues.legal_issue: Investigative lapses alone do not justify acquittal, and the court must independently assess the evidence on record.
material_facts: The investigation involved lapses, including failures concerning the complaints, accused persons’ injuries, weapon seizure and documentation.
The Supreme Court also evaluated the prosecution evidence and found serious contradictions and credibility problems rather than relying on investigative lapses alone.
issues.conclusion: An investigative lapse by itself is not a ground for acquittal; courts must independently assess the evidence and reach a conclusion on whether guilt is proved beyond reasonable doubt.
issues.legal_principle: A court must independently assess the evidence on record and determine whether guilt has been proved beyond reasonable doubt. An investigative officer’s lapse, by itself, is not a ground for acquitting an accused. The Supreme Court did not rely on an earlier case for this principle.

predicates.criminal_case: A court is deciding a prosecution for a criminal offence.
predicates.investigative_lapses: The investigation contains omissions or defects.

issues.definition: In a criminal case involving investigative lapses, the court independently assesses the evidence rather than deciding the case solely on those lapses.

issues.legal_issue: Related eyewitness testimony does not invariably require independent corroboration, but independent evidence is important when the related witnesses’ testimony is incredible and untrustworthy.
material_facts: The eyewitnesses were relatives of the deceased.
The incident occurred on a public road in broad daylight.
The prosecution did not produce reliable independent eyewitness evidence.
The Supreme Court found discrepancies, contradictions and improbable versions in the related witnesses’ testimony.
issues.conclusion: There is no absolute rule requiring corroboration of related witnesses, but in these circumstances the absence of reliable independent evidence reinforced the conclusion that their testimony could not safely support a conviction.
issues.legal_principle: The evidence of a related witness is not subject to an absolute rule requiring corroboration by an independent witness. However, when related eyewitnesses are found incredible and untrustworthy, independent evidence is material to assessing whether their testimony can be relied upon. The Supreme Court did not rely on an earlier case for this principle.

rule.if: criminal_case and related_eyewitnesses and related_testimony_untrustworthy and public_daylight_occurrence and no_reliable_independent_witness

predicates.criminal_case: A court is deciding a prosecution for a criminal offence.
predicates.related_eyewitnesses: The prosecution’s eyewitnesses are related to the victim or otherwise connected to the victim’s side.
predicates.related_testimony_untrustworthy: The court finds the related eyewitnesses’ accounts incredible or not trustworthy.
predicates.public_daylight_occurrence: The incident occurred in a public place in daylight.
predicates.no_reliable_independent_witness: The prosecution did not provide reliable eyewitness evidence from an independent witness.

issues.definition: When related eyewitnesses are found untrustworthy and a public daylight occurrence has no reliable independent eyewitness, their testimony alone is not a safe basis for conviction.

issues.legal_issue: A substantial conflict between medical and eyewitness evidence, when accompanied by serious oral-evidence contradictions and investigative defects, entitles the accused to the benefit of doubt.
material_facts: The doctor testified that the weapons had not been sent for an opinion and that some injuries could have resulted from a fall onto a sharp object or the edge of a drain.

The medical evidence did not support an alleged incised injury to the deceased’s forehead, and the doctor stated that an assault with the alleged weapon would have resulted in a fracture of the frontal bone.
The eyewitness accounts were themselves seriously contradictory, and the handling and seizure of the alleged weapons were uncertain.
issues.conclusion: The combined conflict between the medical and eyewitness evidence, the serious oral contradictions and the investigative defects required that the benefit of doubt go to the accused.
issues.legal_principle: Where medical evidence clearly contradicts ocular evidence and that conflict is accompanied by severe contradictions in oral testimony and clear investigative lapses, the accused are entitled to the benefit of doubt. The Supreme Court did not rely on an earlier case for this principle.

rule.if: criminal_case and material_medical_eyewitness_conflict and serious_oral_contradictions and investigative_lapses

predicates.criminal_case: A court is deciding a prosecution for a criminal offence.
predicates.material_medical_eyewitness_conflict: Medical evidence materially conflicts with the account given by eyewitnesses.
predicates.serious_oral_contradictions: The prosecution witnesses’ accounts contain serious contradictions.
predicates.investigative_lapses: The investigation contains defects that affect the assessment of the prosecution evidence.

issues.definition: In a criminal case, a material conflict between medical and eyewitness evidence, together with serious oral contradictions and investigative lapses, entitles the accused to the benefit of doubt.

issues.legal_issue: Unexplained injuries on an accused can materially undermine the prosecution case when they are supported by medical evidence and arise in circumstances where a complaint was made against the accused’s side.
material_facts: An accused had injuries that were confirmed by a doctor.
A complaint had been made by a family member of an accused against the deceased’s family.
The prosecution did not adequately explain the accused’s injuries, and the investigation did not properly place the related complaint and its disposition before the court.
issues.conclusion: The failure to explain the accused’s injuries and the related investigative omissions were significant defects that, in the circumstances of this case, proved fatal to the prosecution case.
issues.legal_principle: When an accused’s injuries are established and the surrounding circumstances make their explanation material, the prosecution’s failure to explain them may be a serious defect in its case. Here, the Supreme Court considered that failure together with other evidentiary and investigative defects; it did not rely on an earlier case for this principle.

rule.if: criminal_case and accused_injuries_medically_confirmed and injuries_unexplained and related_counter_complaint

predicates.criminal_case: A court is deciding a prosecution for a criminal offence.
predicates.accused_injuries_medically_confirmed: A medical witness confirmed that an accused had injuries.
predicates.injuries_unexplained: The prosecution did not explain how the accused sustained those injuries.
predicates.related_counter_complaint: A complaint was made against the victim’s side concerning the same incident or its surrounding events.

issues.definition: In a criminal case, medically confirmed but unexplained injuries and a related complaint against the victim’s side materially undermine the prosecution case.
